summary:
Everywhere in the world, farmers are watching the rain and the seasons change. What used to be a reliable calendar is now a bet, and a wrong guess can cost a whole harvest.

Cauca Crop Planner turns NASA climate data into a clear answer for every 1 km patch of land: what to plant, when to plant it, and what to grow next to keep the soil alive. We tested it in the Alto Cauca region of Colombia, but it is built on global datasets, so the same idea can grow to any farming region. A small tool, made with care for the people who feed us all.

This first version plans with typical seasonal conditions, not a forecast. As a next step, we plan to add seasonal outlooks (roughly 3 to 6 months ahead), validated with local weather stations

Cauca Crop Planner

Cauca Crop Planner is a web application designed to help smallholder farmers and agricultural extension workers make better planting decisions in the Alto Cauca – Macizo Colombiano region of Colombia. Its main purpose is to answer three important questions for each 1 km² area: Where should farmers plant, when is the best time to do it, and which crops are most suitable? It also helps them decide which crop to grow next through a planned rotation system.

How does it work?

The application brings together satellite data and environmental information from different sources to understand the conditions of each agricultural area. It uses daily climate data from NASA POWER (MERRA-2), including temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind and solar radiation. It also considers elevation through the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 model, adjusting temperature according to altitude, and uses the HydroRIVERS river network to identify areas that may have better access to water for irrigation.

Based on this information, the system evaluates the suitability of four crops: maize, beans, potatoes and peas. It considers factors such as water availability, temperature and crop water requirements, using methods like FAO-56 Penman–Monteith evapotranspiration and Ecocrop-style temperature suitability scores. The final suitability score is determined by the most limiting factor, ensuring that a crop is not recommended when one essential condition is unsuitable.

The system also checks whether these conditions remain favorable throughout the entire growing cycle, rather than considering only the conditions on the planting date. Once suitable areas are identified, a rule-based optimization system suggests between two and four possible crop rotations. These rotations avoid planting crops from the same family consecutively and prioritize legumes before crops with higher nitrogen requirements. Each proposal includes estimated planting and harvesting periods.

To make the information easier to understand, the application includes an interactive map with a biweekly timeline. Farmers can explore how crop suitability changes throughout the year. It also offers a planning mode based on historical climate averages, helping users organize their agricultural activities using typical seasonal conditions rather than relying on a weather forecast.

Benefits and expected impact

Cauca Crop Planner aims to make agricultural planning more accessible by turning complex environmental data into practical recommendations. Instead of relying only on experience or general planting calendars, farmers can explore which crops are more suitable for their specific area and identify better planting periods.

This can help reduce the risk of unsuccessful planting, make better use of available land throughout the year and encourage crop rotation practices that contribute to restoring soil nitrogen and maintaining soil productivity.

Technology and data sources

The application was developed using Python, pandas, NumPy, Streamlit and pydeck, with rasterio and geopandas supporting the preparation and processing of spatial data.

The temperature suitability ranges for maize, beans and peas were checked against FAO Ecocrop and FAO Land & Water references. However, the parameters for potatoes and some crop-cycle values are still preliminary and require further validation.

To make the platform accessible to more users, it includes both English and Spanish language options.

Current limitations

Although the application combines several reliable environmental datasets, there are some limitations to consider. NASA POWER has a spatial resolution of approximately 50 km, which means its climate information may not fully capture the local differences found in mountainous areas such as the Andes. Temperature estimates may have biases of around 1–3 °C, while rainfall data has not yet been locally calibrated.

The current model also does not include soil properties, frost risk or pest and disease conditions. For this reason, its recommendations should be understood as planning guidance rather than definitive agricultural instructions. Any crop management advice should be reviewed and validated by an agronomist familiar with the region.
